source.title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent for Wide Two-layer Neural Networks Trained with the Logistic Loss

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports test-error comparisons for two-layer ReLU networks trained in two ways on synthetic natural labels, but does not test any listed version’s specific intervention or measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical generalization bounds and describes numerical test-error sweeps in Figure 2(b,c). Those sweeps compare training both layers with training only the output layer; the plotted values are figure-only. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports generalization theory and test-error comparisons for training both layers versus only the output layer, but none tests V1–V8. Figure 2(d) measures margin versus width, not held-out error beyond the interpolation threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors characterize different max-margin implicit biases for training both layers versus only the output layer, derive favorable generalization bounds for the former under hidden low-dimensional structure, and report experiments consistent with those benefits. The theoretical characterization requires convergence assumptions; the main smooth-feature theorem excludes ReLU, whose separate treatment requires additional assumptions. General convergence and computational-rate guarantees remain open.
record.recipe_differences: The theory studies infinite-width gradient flow on logistic or exponential-tail losses; the numerical experiments use finite-width ReLU networks and synthetic clustered data with randomly assigned class labels. The test-error figures compare training both layers with training only the output layer.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error comparisons vary training-set size and input dimension, and compare training both layers against training only the output layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 7 reports lower test error when training both layers than when training only the output layer on synthetic clustered data, across training-set-size and input-dimension sweeps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning hidden features can improve generalization over fixed random features on classification problems with hidden low-dimensional structure.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Conference on Learning Theory; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research vol 125
record.problems: The test-error values are presented in plots without numerical values in the text. The numerical experiments use synthetic clustered data, not standard natural-image or language benchmarks. The theorem’s convergence assumptions are not established as generally holding; the paper identifies convergence as an open question.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results qualifying for the listed versions were left out. Figure 2(d) reports F1 margin versus width, which does not measure test error versus width or a training–test gap.

untested.parts: No comparison of fitting example-wise random labels and natural labels with held-out performance. Labels assigned randomly to clusters remain consistent across training and test examples within each cluster.
No held-out-error sweep across widths beyond the width required for zero training error; the width sweep reports normalized training margin.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.
No dropout intervention or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm and margin measures.
No memorization-based example removal and retraining comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Change the record's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. The authors explicitly describe the qualitative test-error advantage, although numerical plot values are unavailable in the supplied text. This advantage does not establish any listed claim version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold; the paper plots F1 margin versus width, not test error versus width.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or other measured properties tracking the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
